questions.prompt: You tested 5 moving-average lengths on 2018-2021 and the 50-day rule scored a Sharpe ratio of 0.95. Why is 0.95 not a fair estimate of how it will do next?
options: Because the Sharpe ratio cannot be annualised
Because 2018-2021 is too short to compute a moving average
Because it is the highest of 5 scores on the same data that picked it
Because the 50-day rule trades too often
questions.explanation: The data that chose the rule also scored it, and you kept the top score. Luck in those 4 years pushed it up, so a later period scored 0.30 instead.

questions.prompt: You checked your rule on the out-of-sample years, did not like the result, changed the rule and checked again. What are those years now?
options: In-sample data, because they helped shape the rule
Still out-of-sample data, because the rule was not fitted to them directly
Better test data, because the rule has been improved
questions.explanation: Out-of-sample data can be used once. Once a result on it changed the rule, it has shaped the design, so it no longer gives a fair judgement.

questions.prompt: Why should the split be by date, with the held-back period last, rather than a random 30% of days?
options: Random splits make the Sharpe ratio negative
Neighbouring days share information, and the held-back part should play the role of the future
pandas cannot select random rows from a time index
A random split always holds back too few days
questions.explanation: With a random split, each held-back day sits next to days used for design. Holding back the last stretch keeps the test like trading a future you have not seen.
